version_history.subject: [PATCH] ipmi:msghandler: Free queued requests of a destroyed user

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch addresses a memory leak issue in the IPMI (Intelligent Platform Management Interface) driver, where requests from destroyed users are not properly freed when the BMC (Baseboard Management Controller) stops responding to IPMI requests. The patch introduces a new function to free queued requests of a destroyed user, preventing the accumulation of closed users and their messages, which can consume significant memory over time. This issue was identified in Meta's fleet, where hosts with malfunctioning BMCs accumulated millions of closed users, leading to memory usage issues. The patch has been tested on QEMU with a fake BMC that stops answering IPMI requests and shows significant reductions in the number of held closed users.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/2] x86/kstack_erase: Use REP STOSQ for large stack fills
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the stack erasure process on x86-64 architecture by using REP STOSQ instruction to fill large spans of memory, which is more efficient than the generic __stackleak_poison() function that uses a word loop. The patch introduces an inline assembly implementation for __stackleak_poison() on x86-64, which fills spans larger than 512 bytes with REP STOSQ and falls back to the word loop for shorter spans. This change reduces the overhead of stack erasure by up to 35% in certain scenarios, making it a performance improvement.

As a matter of interest (and separately from the exact code) how did you
measure the performance to get the 300-400 byte gain point?

If the count is variable - likely in real life, you'll get a branch
misprediction penalty (about 20 clocks on zen5) every time you change
between the two choices.
The copy loop will have another mispredict penalty for the loop itself.

So you are likely to get an overall improvement if you use 'rep stos'
for all lengths - even the ones for with it is slightly slower.
Unless, that is, you know at compile time that most of the length
will be short.

This is particularly beneficial on systems with many small VMs, where the previous implementation was consuming around 1.5% of non-idle kernel cycles. Additionally, the patch includes a build fix for startup code that was causing issues when using Clang and certain configurations.

The change was motivated by benchmarking results that showed significant performance improvements (up to 23% reduction in execution time) compared to the original implementation. Reviewer David Laight noted that the patch's performance results are not conclusive, as they only show a significant improvement for large stack fills and do not account for other factors such as branch prediction, cache behavior, and instruction-level parallelism.

The reviewer, David Laight, notes that the lfence instruction takes long enough to overlap with setup times for REP STOSQ, making it difficult to measure meaningful timings for short operations. He also mentions that the TSC (Time Stamp Counter) doesn't measure clocks accurately and that CPU speed changes during long-running benchmarks. Additionally, he provides benchmark results using PERF_COUNT_CPU_CYCLES counter and direct execution of rdpmc instructions, showing that REP STOSQ is slower than REP MOVSB for large stack fills.
